chief_complaint: jaw pain, malocclusion, and bleeding gums after trauma
hpi_details: A 44-year-old woman presents after facial trauma with jaw pain, malocclusion, and bleeding gums. She reports worsening pain with chewing and is concerned that her teeth no longer meet normally.
ideas: She thinks her jaw slipped out of its joint or that several back teeth were cracked during the blow.
concerns: She is worried that her mouth will have to be wired shut, preventing her from speaking at work and eating solid food.
expectations: She hopes to get a facial X-ray and a prescription for strong painkillers to get through the coming days.

investigation_events.title: Emergency maxillofacial CT
investigation_events.availability_message: The emergency maxillofacial CT result is now available. Continue airway assessment and urgent oral-maxillofacial surgical involvement.

results.value: Displaced fracture through the left mandibular body with a 4 mm step-off and disruption of dental occlusion; no condylar dislocation

core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Mandible Fracture is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.

Standard management emphasizes maxillofacial CT and urgent specialist assessment; closed treatment or open reduction and internal fixation is selected according to fracture pattern, displacement, occlusion, and patient factors.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: jaw pain, malocclusion, and bleeding gums after trauma
Key HPI features: Facial trauma followed by jaw pain, malocclusion, gingival bleeding, and pain with chewing.
Objective/Exam findings: Focused physical exam and vital signs check. Tailored diagnostics for Mandible Fracture.
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Mandible Fracture.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Soft tissue infection without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Missing airway compromise, uncontrolled bleeding, or associated head and cervical-spine injury after facial trauma.
management_principles: Plan for Mandible Fracture: Maxillofacial CT, open reduction and internal fixation (ORIF)
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective: Patient presenting with chief complaint of jaw pain, malocclusion, and bleeding gums after trauma. HPI: facial bone fracture.
reference_soap.objective: Focused physical exam and vital signs check. Tailored diagnostics for Mandible Fracture.
reference_soap.assessment: Condition highly suspicious for Mandible Fracture.
reference_soap.plan: Obtain maxillofacial CT and urgently involve oral and maxillofacial surgery. Manage with closed treatment or ORIF according to fracture pattern, displacement, and occlusion; assess the airway and provide analgesia and oral-care instructions.

learning_objectives: Recognize clinical presentation and diagnostic markers of Mandible Fracture
Select appropriate diagnostic workup for Mandible Fracture
Implement evidence-based management plan: Maxillofacial CT, open reduction and internal fixation (ORIF)

teaching.one_liner: Plastic and reconstructive surgical case presenting with jaw pain, malocclusion, and bleeding gums after trauma.
red_flags: Difficulty breathing, swallowing secretions, drooling, voice change, or uncontrolled oral bleeding requiring immediate airway assessment
Altered consciousness, vomiting, focal neurologic symptoms, or other high-energy trauma requiring emergency evaluation

must_ask.say: How did you injure your jaw, and when did it happen?
Do your teeth fit together the way they used to, and is your lip or chin numb?
Are your gums bleeding, and are you having any trouble breathing or swallowing?

must_ask.objective: Loss of consciousness or associated injuries
must_ask.say: Did you lose consciousness or injure any other part of your body?

must_ask.objective: Alcohol use and prior facial trauma
must_ask.say: Had you been drinking before the injury, and have you had facial trauma before?

history.answer: I tripped and fell on the sidewalk a few hours ago, and now my left jaw hurts terribly, my teeth don't fit together right, and my gums are bleeding.
It happened about three hours ago, right after I fell on the street.
I caught my foot on an uneven sidewalk curb and fell forward, striking the left side of my lower jaw directly against the concrete.
The pain is right along my left lower jawline, and it stays right there without spreading to my neck or ears.
It feels like a deep, throbbing ache at rest that shoots up to a severe sharp pain, about a seven out of ten, whenever I try to speak or bite down.
The pain has been constant since the fall, and the swelling on the left side of my face has been steadily getting worse over the past two hours.
Trying to chew, talk, or close my teeth makes the pain much worse, while keeping my mouth still and holding an ice pack helps ease it slightly.
Yes, my upper and lower teeth don't meet the way they usually do, and it feels completely crooked whenever I try to close my mouth.
The left side of my lower lip and my chin feel numb and tingly, kind of like when dental anesthesia is wearing off.
Yes, I have some blood coming from the gums near my lower left teeth, and a couple of those teeth feel slightly loose.
No, I can breathe fine through my nose and mouth, and I have no trouble swallowing my saliva.
No, I did not pass out or lose consciousness at all, and I have not felt nauseous or vomited.
history.topic: Head injury and loss of consciousness

history.answer: No, I don't have any neck pain, and I didn't hurt my arms, legs, or anywhere else when I fell.
No, my vision is completely normal, with no blurriness or double vision.
No, there is no pain around my ears, and no blood or clear fluid coming out of them.
No, I have never injured my face or broken any bones before this.
I wrapped some ice cubes in a towel to hold against my cheek and used a clean tissue to press on my gums, but I haven't taken any pain medications yet.
I can't chew any solid food, and it hurts so much to talk that I can barely communicate.
I thought my jaw just got knocked out of place or I cracked my molars when I took the impact.
I'm terrified you'll have to wire my jaw shut for weeks, because I can't do my job if I can't speak.
I'm hoping to get an X-ray to see what's broken and some strong pain medicine so I can actually manage to swallow.
I don't have any chronic medical conditions like high blood pressure, diabetes, or bleeding disorders.
I have never had any surgeries or been admitted to a hospital.
I am not taking any prescription medicines, over-the-counter drugs, or herbal supplements.
I don't have any known allergies to medications.
I have never smoked cigarettes or used any tobacco products.
I only drink socially, maybe a single glass of wine once or twice a month, and I had not had any alcohol before I fell today.
I work as an accountant at an office, and I live with my husband and teenage daughter.
There is no history of bone disorders or chronic illnesses in my family.
My last menstrual period started about two weeks ago, my cycles are regular, and there is no chance I am pregnant because my husband had a vasectomy.

exam.finding: Alert, in mild distress holding an ice pack against the left jaw, speaking carefully, with no signs of airway compromise.
Blood pressure 128/82 mmHg, heart rate 82 beats/min, respiratory rate 16 breaths/min, temperature 36.8°C, oxygen saturation 99% on room air.
Alert and fully oriented to person, place, and time with clear thought processes.
Ecchymosis and a palpable step-off deformity with localized tenderness along the left mandibular body; jaw opening is limited to 20 mm.
Mild gingival laceration with active oozing and dental step-off between the left lower premolars, malocclusion on biting, and no pharyngeal hematoma or airway obstruction.
Decreased sensation to light touch over the left lower lip and chin in the mental nerve distribution; facial motor function is symmetric and intact.
External auditory canals are clear bilaterally with no blood, laceration, or cerebrospinal fluid leak.
Pupils are equal, round, and reactive to light; extraocular movements are intact without diplopia, and orbital rims are intact.
No cervical spine tenderness, deformity, or paraspinal muscle spasm.
